lessons.title: Revelation, Visions and Miracles as Proof of God

before.content_html:
What Is Revelation?

Revelation is the means by which God makes himself known. Catholics believe God has revealed himself progressively throughout history — through the natural world, through the prophets and scriptures of the Old Testament, and most completely through Jesus Christ. The letter to the Hebrews captures this: “In the past God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets at many times and in various ways, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things” (Hebrews 1:1–4). For Catholics, Jesus is not just one revelation among many — he is the fullness of revelation, the definitive Word of God.

This teaching shapes how Catholics read the whole Bible. The Old Testament points forward to Christ; the New Testament shows Christ as the fulfilment of everything the prophets promised. For a Catholic student today, this means that every act of worship, every scripture reading, and every sacrament is understood as an encounter with the God who has already fully revealed himself in Jesus.

Key Fact

Hebrews 1:1–4 teaches that God spoke through the prophets in many ways, but in “these last days” has spoken through his Son. Catholics use this verse to argue that Jesus is the culmination of divine revelation — making Christianity the fullest expression of God’s self-disclosure to humanity.

Visions as Proof of God

Visions have played a significant role in the Catholic tradition as evidence that God is real and communicates with human beings. The Bible records visions that shaped key figures in salvation history. In Genesis 15, God appears to Abraham in a vision, promising him descendants as numerous as the stars — the covenant that defines the whole people of Israel. In Matthew 17:1–13, Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James and John on a high mountain: his face shines like the sun, his clothes become dazzling white, and Moses and Elijah appear alongside him. The disciples hear God’s voice from a cloud: “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased. Listen to him!” This vision of the Transfiguration confirmed the disciples’ faith in Jesus as the Son of God.

Beyond scripture, non-biblical visions have also shaped Catholic faith. The most studied is that of Joan of Arc, who reported visions of St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret from around 1425, instructing her to support the French King Charles VII. The Catholic Church canonised Joan in 1920, recognising her life and reported visions as holy. For Catholics, such approved visions are not the basis of new doctrine but can deepen personal faith and confirm existing beliefs.

Atheists and Humanists argue that visions provide no proof that God exists. They point to natural explanations: visions may be hallucinations caused by hunger, illness, psychological distress, or brain activity during sleep. The Humanist argument is that a vision is an internal, subjective experience — it cannot be verified by anyone else, and the content of visions consistently reflects the cultural expectations of the visionary (a medieval French girl sees Catholic saints; a first-century Jew sees angels). Richard Dawkins and other atheist writers argue that the brain is capable of generating extraordinarily vivid experiences that feel external and real but are not. Catholics respond that the consistency, moral transformation, and in some cases miraculous healings associated with visions cannot be explained away so easily, and that subjective experience is still genuine data about reality.

Miracles as Proof of God

A miracle is an event that seems to go beyond natural explanation and points to the direct action of God. Catholics believe miracles demonstrate that God is active in the world and confirm the truth of the faith. The Gospel of John records an example: in John 4:43–54, Jesus heals a royal official’s son who is near death, doing so at a distance without being physically present. When the man checks the timing, he finds his son began to recover at the exact moment Jesus spoke. This sign strengthened his household’s faith.

The most famous modern site of Catholic miracles is Lourdes, a town in southern France. Since 1858, when the Virgin Mary reportedly appeared to Bernadette Soubirous, millions of pilgrims have visited. The Lourdes Medical Bureau investigates claimed healings rigorously; the Catholic Church has officially recognised 70 cures as miraculous since 1858, meaning no scientific or medical explanation has been found. These are not accepted uncritically — each case is examined by doctors of all faiths and none before Church recognition.

Key Fact

Lourdes is the principal Catholic site of miraculous healing. The Virgin Mary reportedly appeared to Bernadette Soubirous in 1858. The Lourdes Medical Bureau has recognised 70 miracles since then. For Catholics, these unexplained healings are evidence that God acts directly in the world and that Catholic faith is true.

Atheist and Humanist arguments against miracles take several forms. First, they argue that modern science can explain events that earlier ages attributed to divine intervention — what once seemed miraculous is now understood as remission, psychosomatic healing, or misdiagnosis. Second, they argue that reports of miracles are unreliable and based on anecdote and wishful thinking rather than rigorous evidence. Third, philosophers like David Hume argued in the eighteenth century that the uniform experience of natural law gives us stronger grounds to doubt a miracle report than to accept it — it is always more likely that a witness is mistaken than that a law of nature was broken. Catholics respond that Hume’s argument assumes the outcome before examining the evidence, and that the verified Lourdes cases have withstood medical scrutiny. They also argue that even if science one day explains every healing, that need not rule out God as the cause working through natural processes.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Catholics believe revelation reached its fullness in Jesus Christ, as stated in Hebrews 1:1–4 — this makes Jesus not just one source of knowledge about God among many, but the definitive Word of God.
  • Visions such as the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–13) and Joan of Arc’s visions are used as evidence for God’s existence and communication with humanity, though atheists argue visions have natural neurological explanations.
  • Miracles at Lourdes, including 70 Church-recognised healings since 1858, are presented as evidence of divine action; Humanists and atheists respond that unexplained does not mean supernatural.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark “Explain Two with Sources” question, you must name a specific source — for example, “In Hebrews 1:1–4, the writer teaches that God has spoken most fully through his Son” or “John 4:43–54 records Jesus healing the official’s son at a distance.” A paraphrase without the reference earns only 4 marks at most. For the 12-mark “Discuss” question, make sure you develop the atheist or Humanist counter-argument fully — examiners consistently note that students write only one sentence on the opposing view. Give two developed points on each side, use evaluative language like “however” and “this is more convincing because,” and reach a justified conclusion. SPaG marks reward correct spelling of technical terms: “revelation,” “Transfiguration,” “miracle.”

practice_questions.text: Outline three Catholic beliefs about revelation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points, for example: God has revealed himself through the Old Testament prophets; God revealed himself most fully through Jesus Christ (Hebrews 1:1-4); God's revelation is ongoing through the Church and scripture; the natural world reflects God's presence and is a form of general revelation. Three distinct points required; elaboration of one point does not earn three marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe the miracle of the healing of the royal official's son as recorded in John 4:43-54.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks for accurate description: a royal official asked Jesus to heal his son who was near death (1); Jesus told him to go home, that his son would live, without travelling to him (1); when the official checked the timing, his son's recovery began at the exact hour Jesus spoke (1). Full marks require three accurate details.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Catholics believe visions provide evidence for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Visions often result in moral transformation and deepened faith in those who experience them, suggesting they come from a source beyond the human mind (2); The consistency between biblical visions (Genesis 15, Matthew 17) and later visions shows a pattern of divine communication rather than random hallucination (2). Other valid reasoning accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Catholics believe the miracles at Lourdes support belief in God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for first reason with development; 2 marks for second reason with development; 1 mark for a named source of wisdom or authority. For example: The 70 Church-recognised miracles have withstood medical investigation by doctors of all faiths, and no natural explanation has been found, suggesting divine action (2); John 4:43-54 records Jesus performing a miracle at a distance, establishing a precedent that God can act beyond the limits of the natural world, which Catholics see reflected at Lourdes (2); source credit for citing John 4:43-54 or Hebrews 1:1-4 explicitly (1). A paraphrased source without a named reference does not earn the fifth mark.

practice_questions.text:
'Miracles at places like Lourdes are the strongest evidence Catholics have for the existence of God.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; argument weighs perspectives explicitly; conclusion justifies a clear position. May argue Lourdes miracles are strong evidence (70 officially recognised healings, independent medical investigation, John 4:43-54 biblical precedent) but evaluate whether this beats other arguments (cosmological, design, religious experience) or whether atheist rebuttals (Hume, natural explanations) undermine the case. Secure (7-9): Both sides present with some development; at least one named source; conclusion present but may not weigh the evidence explicitly. Developing (4-6): One side more developed; sources vague or absent; conclusion descriptive. Emerging (1-3): One-sided; very brief; no named sources. SPaG marks reward correct use of theological vocabulary: miracle, revelation, Lourdes, Transfiguration.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which visions have been important in Catholic history, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per way (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation); 1 mark for a named source. For example: The Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-13) confirmed the disciples' belief in Jesus as the Son of God by revealing his divine glory alongside Moses and Elijah (2); Joan of Arc's visions guided her to support the French king and led to her eventual canonisation in 1920, showing the Church accepts non-biblical visions when they are confirmed by holy living (2); source credit for Matthew 17:1-13 or Genesis 15 named explicitly (1).

lessons.title: Religious Experience, the Design Argument and the Cosmological Argument

before.content_html:
Religious Experience as Evidence for God

Religious experience refers to moments when a person feels they have encountered God directly. Catholics believe such experiences are a genuine route to knowledge of God, though the Church exercises caution — not every claimed experience is accepted as authentic. The Catechism of the Catholic Church at paragraphs 66–67 teaches that although God’s revelation in Christ is complete, private revelations and religious experiences can “help us live more fully by it” in a particular era. Crucially, the Catechism makes clear that no new public revelation is possible after Jesus: private religious experiences cannot add to or override the deposit of faith.

Atheists and Humanists challenge the evidential value of religious experiences. They argue that a subjective inner experience — however powerful — is not verifiable evidence that God exists. The same brain states that produce a religious experience could, in their view, be produced by meditation, sleep deprivation, or psychological suggestion. Dawkins argues in The God Delusion that religious experience reflects the brain’s tendency to detect agency and pattern, not a real encounter with God. Catholics respond that the moral transformation, lasting peace, and convergence across cultures of religious experiences point to something real beyond neurological processes.

Key Fact

Catechism of the Catholic Church 66–67 teaches that God’s revelation is complete in Christ, but private revelations (including religious experiences) can help believers live more fully by it. The Church insists that no private revelation adds to the deposit of faith — it can only deepen understanding of what has already been revealed.

The Design Argument

The design argument (also called the teleological argument) proposes that the order, complexity and beauty of the natural world are best explained by an intelligent designer. Paul states in Romans 1:18–24 that “since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities — his eternal power and divine nature — have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made.” For Catholics, this verse establishes that the natural world itself reveals God to those who look carefully.

The most celebrated version of the design argument comes from William Paley, who published Natural Theology in 1802. Paley argued using the watchmaker analogy: if you found a watch on a heath, you would conclude it had a designer because of its intricate, purposeful construction. Paley argued that living organisms — eyes, hearts, wings — are far more complex than any watch. They must therefore have a designer vastly more intelligent than any human craftsman: God.

Richard Dawkins, in The Blind Watchmaker (1986), argues that natural selection entirely explains apparent design without any designer. Evolution shows that complexity can accumulate gradually through random mutation and differential survival — no intelligence is required. Dawkins calls Paley “gloriously and utterly wrong.” Humanists add that the natural world also contains enormous amounts of what looks like bad design: vestigial organs, disease, predation, extinction. If a designer made the universe, they argue, it is not an all-loving, all-powerful God. Catholics respond that evolution is compatible with Catholic teaching (the Church does not reject it) and that the laws of physics governing evolution still point to a lawgiver. Cardinal Newman famously argued that the orderliness of the cosmos — the fact that evolution follows predictable laws — is itself evidence of a rational mind behind nature.

Aquinas’s First Three Ways: The Cosmological Argument

The cosmological argument argues that the existence of the universe requires a cause outside itself. The most celebrated Catholic version comes from Thomas Aquinas, whose Summa Theologica presents five arguments. The spec focuses on the first three, which are all forms of the cosmological argument.

Key Fact

Aquinas’s First Three Ways are: (1) the argument from motion (everything in motion was put in motion by something else — there must be an unmoved mover, God); (2) the argument from causation (everything has a cause — there must be a first uncaused cause, God); (3) the argument from contingency (things in the universe exist but might not — there must be a necessary being, God, who cannot fail to exist). All three are a posteriori: they begin from observation of the world and reason to God.

The prime mover is the conclusion of the First Way. Aquinas observed that everything in the universe is in motion or in a state of change. For something to change, it must be acted upon by something already in the relevant state. You cannot have an infinite chain going backwards — at some point, there must be something that initiates motion without itself being moved. This first mover is what Catholics call God. The argument from contingency takes a different angle: the universe did not have to exist. Its existence demands explanation; that explanation is a being whose existence is necessary rather than contingent — God.

Students regularly confuse three distinct philosophical arguments. Aquinas’s First Three Ways are a posteriori (starting from observation of the world: motion, causation, contingency) and conclude to God as first mover, first cause, and necessary being. The Ontological Argument, by contrast, was devised by St Anselm of Canterbury in his Proslogion (c.1078) and is a priori (based on the concept of God alone, not observation). Anselm’s argument is NOT in the Edexcel spec for Paper 3 — do not bring it in. The Kalam cosmological argument (“everything that begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; therefore the universe has a cause”) is the Islamic version associated with al-Ghazali — covered in the Islam route, not here. Aquinas and al-Ghazali made different arguments and lived in different centuries. Never attribute the Kalam to Aquinas or the Five Ways to al-Ghazali.
before.exam_tip_html: The most common error on questions about the cosmological argument is confusing Aquinas’s First Three Ways with the Ontological Argument (Anselm) or the Kalam (al-Ghazali). For this paper, you need Aquinas: First Way (motion), Second Way (causation), Third Way (contingency). These are all observations from the world, not logical proofs from the concept of God alone. For the 5-mark source question, Romans 1:18–24 is the named anchor for the design argument: cite the book, chapter and verse range. For the 12-mark Discuss, develop the Dawkins/evolution challenge in full — do not just mention it in passing — and respond to it from the Catholic position. SPaG marks reward precise spelling of: cosmological, contingency, teleological.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Aquinas's cosmological argument for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points from: everything in motion was put in motion by something else, so there must be an unmoved mover (1); everything has a cause, so there must be a first uncaused cause (1); contingent things could have not existed, so there must be a necessary being (1). Three distinct points required.

practice_questions.text: Describe William Paley's watchmaker analogy.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Paley argued that if you found a watch on a heath, its complexity would imply a watchmaker (1); he applied this to living organisms such as the eye, which are even more complex and purposeful than a watch (1); therefore the natural world must also have a designer — God (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Catholics use religious experience as evidence for the existence of God.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Religious experiences produce lasting moral transformation and peace, suggesting they originate from God rather than the human mind alone (2); The Catechism (CCC 66-67) recognises that private revelations, though adding nothing to doctrine, can deepen faith and help believers live more fully by God's revelation (2). Other valid reasoning accepted.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic reasons for believing the design argument supports belief in God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason with development; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The natural world shows clear evidence of order and purpose — eyes, ecosystems, physical constants — which is best explained by an intelligent creator rather than chance (2); Romans 1:18-24 explicitly states that God's eternal power and divine nature have been 'clearly seen' in the created world, lending scriptural support to the design argument (2); source credit for naming Romans 1:18-24 (1).

practice_questions.text:
'The cosmological argument is the most convincing proof of the existence of God.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing of arguments; justified conclusion. May argue the cosmological argument is strong because it begins from observable facts (not mere logic) and Aquinas's Three Ways are logically coherent, but evaluate whether it is more or less convincing than the design argument or religious experience; address Humanist and atheist rebuttals (infinite regress question, 'who made God' objection). Secure (7-9): Both sides present, at least one source, conclusion present but evaluative language limited. Developing (4-6): One side dominant, vague sources, descriptive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided, no sources. SPaG: cosmological, contingency, Aquinas, teleological.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some people argue the design argument does not prove God exists, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Darwin's theory of evolution (On the Origin of Species, 1859) shows that complexity in living organisms arises through natural selection, not design — Dawkins argues this removes the need for a designer (2); the presence of suffering, disease and extinction in nature looks like poor design, making it hard to attribute the world to an all-loving, all-powerful God (2); source credit for naming Romans 1:18-24 in counter-argument framing, or naming Dawkins The Blind Watchmaker, or Darwin (1).

lessons.title: The Problem of Evil and Catholic Responses

before.exam_tip_html: The most dangerous error on problem-of-evil questions is swapping Augustine and Irenaeus. Fix this now: Augustine = free-will defence + privation of good + the Fall. Irenaeus (developed by Hick) = soul-making + moral development. For the 5-mark source question, cite the Psalm (e.g. “Psalm 119 shows the writer turning to God’s word in suffering”) or Job as your source — these are the named biblical anchors in the spec. For the 12-mark Discuss, develop the Humanist counter-argument in full: they argue that theodicies are unconvincing because the scale of suffering is too great, or because natural evil cannot be explained by free will. Respond from the Catholic position. SPaG marks: spell “theodicy,” “privation,” “omnipotent,” “omniscient” correctly.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which suffering challenges Catholic belief in God.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: if God is all-powerful he could prevent suffering (1); if God is all-loving he would want to prevent suffering (1); the existence of natural evil (earthquakes, disease) which humans did not cause makes it hard to attribute suffering to human free will alone (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe Augustine's free-will defence of God in the face of evil.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Augustine argues evil is not a thing God created but the privation (absence) of good (1); evil entered the world through the Fall — humanity's free choice to disobey God (1); God gave humans free will because freely chosen love is more valuable than compelled love, but this freedom was misused (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Augustine's free-will defence and the Irenaean soul-making theodicy.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: Augustine sees evil as the result of a fall from an original state of perfection — humans were created good but chose evil; Irenaeus sees humans as created immature and needing to develop, so suffering is part of the growth process rather than a consequence of a fall (2); Augustine's theodicy focuses on the origin of evil (the Fall) whereas Irenaeus (developed by Hick) focuses on the purpose of evil (moral development/soul-making) (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic responses to the problem of evil, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per response with development; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Prayer — Psalm 119 models the response of turning to God's word in suffering and trusting in his ultimate goodness even when circumstances suggest abandonment (2); Charity — Catholics address suffering practically, following Jesus's example and teachings such as Matthew 25:31-46 which calls Christians to care for the vulnerable (2); source credit for citing Psalm 119, Job, or another named biblical reference explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'The soul-making theodicy gives a more convincing response to the problem of evil than Augustine's free-will defence.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; argument weighs both theodicies and responds to challenges; justified conclusion. May argue soul-making (Irenaeus/Hick) is stronger because it gives purpose to natural evil, not just moral evil, and addresses why God allows suffering rather than just where it came from. Counter: Augustine's privation argument is philosophically coherent and grounded in the Fall narrative; Hick's model faces the disproportionality problem (Holocaust). Both may be challenged as inadequate. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, at least one source. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: theodicy, privation, Augustine, Irenaeus.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why some people argue that theodicies fail to solve the problem of evil, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Natural evil (disease, earthquakes) cannot easily be attributed to human free will — viruses do not choose to harm, making Augustine's free-will defence incomplete (2); the scale of suffering — including events like the Holocaust — seems vastly disproportionate to any developmental need, undermining the soul-making theodicy (2); source credit for Job (the Bible's most direct engagement with disproportionate suffering) or Psalm 119 cited explicitly (1).

before.content_html:
Marriage as a Sacrament

Marriage occupies a central place in Catholic life. For Catholics, marriage is not simply a social or legal arrangement — it is a sacrament of marriage, one of the seven sacraments through which God’s grace is communicated. The couple are themselves the ministers of the sacrament — they confer it on each other through their freely given, permanent vows, witnessed by the priest and community. The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2360–2365 sets out the essential properties of marriage: unity (one husband, one wife), indissolubility (lifelong commitment) and openness to procreation.

Pope Francis addressed the meaning of marriage in his speech “Not Just Good But Beautiful” at the Humanum Conference in November 2014. He described marriage as a “beautiful” vocation that reflects the covenant between Christ and the Church, and lamented that contemporary culture has reduced marriage to a transient arrangement rather than a total gift of self. For Catholics, the permanence of the marriage vow — “what God has joined together, let no one separate” — is a reflection of the faithful, unconditional love of God himself.

Key Fact

Pope Francis’s address “Not Just Good But Beautiful” was given at the Humanum Conference in November 2014. It presents Catholic marriage as beautiful because it reflects Christ’s covenant with the Church — total, permanent and fruitful. It is one of the Edexcel-named sources for Catholic teaching on marriage.

Sexual Relationships: Marital, Unitive and Procreative

Catholic teaching holds that sexual relationships are only appropriate within marriage. The Catechism (CCC 2360–2365) identifies three essential dimensions of marital sexuality. First, sex is marital — confined to the marriage relationship. Second, it is unitive — it deepens and expresses the loving bond between spouses, strengthening the covenant. Third, it is procreative — it must remain open to new life. Catholic teaching insists that the unitive and procreative dimensions cannot be artificially separated. To remove the procreative dimension deliberately (as artificial contraception does) is to violate the full meaning of the sexual act.

On same-sex relationships, the Catechism teaches that while individuals with same-sex attraction deserve respect and compassion, same-sex sexual activity does not correspond to the marital vocation as the Church understands it. This is one of the most debated areas of Catholic ethics in contemporary society, with divergent views within Christianity: many Protestant denominations and the Church of England now affirm same-sex partnerships, reflecting a different interpretation of scripture and tradition. Catholics are called to treat everyone with dignity while maintaining the teaching on marriage.

Many Protestant churches and some Anglican denominations accept sexual relationships outside marriage and same-sex partnerships, arguing that love and commitment are the core Christian values rather than the legal form. Non-religious (Humanist and atheist) views generally hold that consensual sexual relationships between adults are morally acceptable regardless of marital status, and that human wellbeing and equality are the key ethical tests. The Catholic Church responds that its teaching is grounded in natural law (the purpose of sex as written into human nature) and in scripture, not merely in social convention, and that redefining marriage or sexuality ultimately harms human flourishing even if it appears liberating in the short term.

The Purpose and Importance of Family

For Catholics, the family is “the domestic church” — the first place where faith is lived and passed on. The primary purposes of marriage include procreation and the education of children in the faith. Familiaris Consortio (Pope John Paul II, 1981), sections 36–85, provides the most detailed modern Catholic teaching on the family. It describes the family as the “first and vital cell of society” and outlines four specific tasks: forming a community of persons, serving life, participating in the development of society, and sharing in the life and mission of the Church.

Catholics do not ignore the reality of diverse family structures in 21st-century society. The Church recognises that families today include nuclear, single-parent, same-sex parent, extended, and blended families. The Catholic response is pastoral rather than condemnatory — families who do not match the ideal are still offered the full support of the Church community, while the Church maintains its teaching about the ideal of marriage between a man and a woman.

Key Fact

Familiaris Consortio was written by Pope John Paul II in 1981. It describes the family as the “first and vital cell of society” and the “domestic church.” It gives four tasks of the family: community of persons, serving life, developing society, and sharing in the Church’s mission. Sections 36–85 cover the family directly.

Support from the Local Parish: Family Group Movement

The local Catholic parish supports families through family worship, sacramental preparation, parents’ classes, children’s groups and counselling. One concrete example the spec names is the Family Group Movement, founded in France in 1947. Small groups of families meet regularly for prayer, discussion and practical support, creating a community in which faith can be shared and family life strengthened. The Catechism 2226 also notes that parents are “the first educators” of their children in the faith — the parish exists to support them in that primary vocation, not to replace it.

Cohabitation (living together as an unmarried couple) is viewed negatively in official Catholic teaching, because the permanence and public commitment of marriage are seen as essential to the full meaning of the sexual relationship. Many non-religious people and some Protestants regard cohabitation as a reasonable way to test compatibility before marriage, and argue that committed relationships have the same moral value whether legally formalised or not. The Catholic Church responds that the absence of a binding commitment changes the nature of the relationship and undermines the conditions for genuine self-gift. It nevertheless recognises that pastoral sensitivity is required when working with cohabiting couples who may be seeking to grow closer to the Church.

lessons.title: Contraception, Divorce, Gender Equality and Discrimination

before.content_html:
Family Planning and Contraception

The Catholic Church teaches that artificial contraception is morally wrong. This position is most clearly stated in Humanae Vitae (1968), written by Pope Paul VI. The document argues that every act of sexual intercourse must remain open to both its unitive dimension (deepening love between spouses) and its procreative dimension (openness to new life). Deliberately removing the procreative dimension through artificial means — the contraceptive pill, condoms, sterilisation — violates the integrity of the sexual act as God intended it.

The Church does not oppose natural family planning (NFP), which works with the body’s natural fertility cycles. NFP methods (such as monitoring the woman’s cycle to identify fertile and infertile periods) are not considered contraception in the moral sense because no act of intercourse is deliberately made infertile — instead, couples abstain during fertile periods. Catholics who use NFP still respect the principle that each act of intercourse must remain open to life in principle.

Key Fact

Humanae Vitae was published in 1968 by Pope Paul VI. It forbids the use of artificial contraception on the grounds that the unitive and procreative dimensions of marriage cannot be artificially separated. It remains one of the most debated documents in modern Catholic history.

Most Protestant denominations, including the Church of England, accept artificial contraception as a responsible way to plan a family. They argue that responsible parenthood and the wellbeing of existing children and the mother are important factors that a fixed rule about every act cannot accommodate. From the perspective of situation ethics (Joseph Fletcher, 1966), each case should be decided by what maximises love (agape) — and for a couple in poverty or with health concerns, contraception may be the most loving choice. Humanists and atheists generally see contraception as a tool of responsible reproductive choice with no moral problem. Catholics respond that the Church’s teaching is not merely a rule but a statement about the nature of sexual love, and that following it requires virtue, not restriction.

Divorce, Annulment and Remarriage

Divorce is not recognised by the Catholic Church as a valid dissolution of a sacramental marriage. Because marriage is a sacrament — a permanent covenant before God — it cannot simply be dissolved by a civil court. The Catechism of the Catholic Church 2382–2386 acknowledges that civil divorce may sometimes be justified as a legal measure to protect financial and civil rights, particularly in cases of abuse or abandonment. But in Catholic teaching, the person remains married before God even after a civil divorce. Remarrying while a first spouse is still living is therefore regarded as adultery.

The Church does, however, offer the process of annulment. This is not the same as divorce — it does not dissolve a marriage but declares that a valid sacramental marriage never existed from the beginning, because one or both parties lacked the capacity, freedom or intention required for a valid marriage. If a marriage is annulled, both parties are free to marry in the Church. Annulments require an investigation by a Church tribunal and are not automatic.

Key Fact

Catechism 2382–2386: civil divorce does not dissolve a sacramental marriage before God. Remarriage after divorce without annulment is regarded as adultery. Annulment is the Church’s ruling that a valid sacramental marriage never existed — not a Catholic divorce. Distinction is crucial in the exam.

Equality of Men and Women in the Family

Catholic teaching holds that men and women are equal in dignity before God but have complementary roles in the family. Catechism 2207 states that the family is “the original cell of social life” and that within the family, both parents have essential roles. The Church values what it calls “the dignity of work within the home” — the contribution of whoever carries out domestic and childcare work, whether mother or father, is considered genuinely valuable and not less important than paid employment.

Pope John Paul II’s “theology of the body” (a series of catechetical lectures given 1979–1984) offers a deeper philosophical framework. John Paul II argued that the body itself is a “theology” — its sexual differentiation as male and female reflects the self-giving love that defines the Trinity and that finds its human expression in marriage. This approach respects the embodied difference between men and women while insisting on their equal dignity and worth.

Gender Prejudice and Discrimination

The Catholic Church officially opposes all forms of gender prejudice and discrimination. Catechism 1938 states that “every form of social or cultural discrimination in fundamental personal rights on the grounds of sex, race, color, social conditions, language, or religion must be curbed and eradicated as incompatible with God’s design.” This is a strong and explicit statement. Within Catholic families and communities, both men and women should be treated with equal respect and given equal opportunity to develop their gifts.

The question of the role of women in the Church is a point of divergence within Christianity. The Catholic and Orthodox churches do not ordain women as priests, arguing that Jesus chose only male apostles and that this reflects a permanent theological intention, not a cultural accident. The Church of England and most Protestant denominations do ordain women, arguing that the principle of equality in Christ (“there is neither male nor female” — Galatians 3:28) outweighs the argument from historical practice. Catholics respond that women hold vitally important roles in the Church as religious sisters, catechists, liturgical ministers and leaders of lay movements, even without ordination.

Situation ethics, developed by Joseph Fletcher in 1966, argues that love (agape) should guide every moral decision contextually, without rigid rules. Applied to divorce, this might mean that if a marriage has irretrievably broken down and both parties are suffering, the most loving course is separation and the freedom to remarry. Applied to gender roles, situation ethicists would argue that whatever enables human beings to flourish and love one another is morally correct, regardless of traditional role boundaries. Catholics respond that situation ethics sounds compassionate but can justify almost any action if framed in terms of “love,” and that the natural law framework of Catholic ethics provides more reliable guidance for human flourishing over time than case-by-case judgement.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Humanae Vitae (Pope Paul VI, 1968) forbids artificial contraception: every act of sex must remain open to life. Natural family planning is permitted because it works with fertility rather than against it.
  • Catholic teaching (CCC 2382–2386) does not recognise divorce of a valid sacramental marriage. Annulment declares a marriage was never valid; it is not divorce. Remarriage after divorce without annulment is considered adultery.
  • Men and women are equal in dignity (CCC 1938 opposes all gender discrimination). Pope John Paul II’s theology of the body argues that the body’s sexual complementarity reflects the self-giving love of the Trinity.
before.exam_tip_html: The two most important named sources for this lesson are Humanae Vitae (Pope Paul VI, 1968) on contraception and Catechism 2382–2386 on divorce and annulment. In the exam, state these precisely: “In Humanae Vitae (1968), Pope Paul VI taught that artificial contraception violates the unitive and procreative nature of marriage.” For gender, the source is Catechism 1938 (opposition to discrimination) and Catechism 2207 (family as cell of society). Do not confuse annulment with divorce — annulment declares a marriage was never valid; divorce dissolves a valid marriage. The Catholic Church recognises the former but not the latter. SPaG marks: spell Humanae Vitae, “annulment,” “contraception” correctly.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Catholic teachings about divorce.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by civil divorce (1); civil divorce may be permitted as a legal protection but does not dissolve the marriage before God (1); remarriage after divorce without annulment is regarded as adultery (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe Catholic teaching on artificial contraception as set out in Humanae Vitae.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Humanae Vitae (1968) by Pope Paul VI teaches that artificial contraception is morally wrong (1); because each act of sexual intercourse must remain open to both its unitive and procreative dimensions (1); deliberately removing the procreative dimension through artificial means violates the integrity of marriage (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between a Catholic annulment and a civil divorce.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: A civil divorce dissolves a legally valid marriage, whereas a Catholic annulment declares that no valid sacramental marriage ever existed from the beginning — it is not a dissolution but a declaration (2); after an annulment, both parties are free to marry in the Catholic Church, whereas after a civil divorce without annulment, remarriage in the Church is not permitted (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic teachings about the equality of men and women, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per teaching with development; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Catechism 1938 explicitly states that 'every form of social or cultural discrimination in fundamental personal rights on the grounds of sex... must be curbed and eradicated as incompatible with God's design' — showing the Church's commitment to gender equality (2); Catechism 2207 values the dignity of work within the home, recognising that domestic and childcare work is as valuable as paid employment for both men and women (2); source credit for naming CCC 1938, CCC 2207, or theology of the body by Pope John Paul II (1).

practice_questions.text:
'The Catholic Church is right to forbid artificial contraception.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Catholic view: Humanae Vitae (1968, Paul VI) argues that separating unitive and procreative dimensions violates the nature of marriage; natural law supports this. Counter: most Protestant churches accept contraception as responsible family planning; situation ethics (Fletcher, 1966) would say the loving choice should guide each case; Humanists argue reproductive autonomy is a basic right. Evaluate which case is stronger. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: Humanae Vitae, contraception, procreative.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which divergent Christian views about divorce and remarriage differ from Catholic teaching, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Many Protestant churches allow divorce and remarriage, arguing that the compassionate response to an irretrievably broken marriage is freedom to begin again rather than lifelong legal commitment to a dead relationship (2); the Catholic Church, by contrast, teaches that CCC 2382-2386 does not permit remarriage after divorce of a valid sacramental marriage, as marriage is a permanent covenant before God (2); source credit for CCC 2382-2386 or Humanae Vitae cited explicitly (1).
